meta.blurb: Ten questions a curious child might ask, and the honest answers: how big the universe is, how it began, what it is made of, how it ends, what time is, and whether we are alone. Learn what science knows, how it knows it, and what it still cannot say.
meta.bible: This book asks ten big questions about the universe, five pages for each: how big is it, how did it begin, what is it made of, how will it end, what is time, what is gravity, are there other Earths, are we alone, what is a black hole, and what do we not know. Key terms: Universe, Galaxy, Galaxies, Atoms, Atom, Hydrogen, Helium, Carbon, Oxygen, Iron, Electrons, Nucleus, Light-year, Milky Way, Big Bang, Dark matter, Dark energy, Relativity, Gravity, Gravitational, Exoplanets, Exoplanet, Telescope, Telescopes, Singularity, Event horizon, Cosmic, Microwave, Radio, Spectrum, Spectrographs, Planet, Orbit, Antenna, Eclipse, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Europa, Enceladus, Quantum, Physicists, Astronomers. People and events (real): Albert Einstein (theory of relativity, 1915; the eclipse test of 1919); Isaac Newton (gravity, late 1600s); Vera Rubin (measured galaxy rotation in the 1970s); two radio engineers found the cosmic microwave background in 1965. Facts used: the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away; the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away; a light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres; the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across with hundreds of billions of stars; the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across; the Big Bang was about 13.8 billion years ago; atoms formed about 380,000 years after it; ordinary matter is about 5 percent, dark matter about 27 percent and dark energy about 68 percent (estimates); expansion speeding up found in 1998; the Sun has about five billion years left; the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star was found in 1995 and more than 5,000 are known; gravitational waves were first detected in 2015; the first black hole image came in 2019 (the galaxy M87) and the Milky Way's in 2022. Voice: clear, friendly and honest; always say what is known, how we know it, and what is still unknown. Every number is real or marked as about; no invented facts.

beats.scene: A person lies on a hillside at night under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Introduction: ten big questions about the universe, and the first one, how big it is.

beats.scene: The Earth, the Moon and the Sun in a line, with distances marked
beats.summary: Distances grow quickly: the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away and the Sun about 150 million.

beats.scene: A beam of light crosses a dark space marked with years
beats.summary: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about nine and a half trillion kilometres, and astronomers use it as a ruler.

beats.scene: A spiral of billions of stars glows against the darkness of space
beats.summary: Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is about a hundred thousand light-years across and holds hundreds of billions of stars.

beats.scene: A tiny patch of dark sky is filled with thousands of colourful galaxies
beats.summary: Beyond the Milky Way there are hundreds of billions more galaxies, and the observable universe is about ninety-three billion light-years across, but the whole universe may be larger.

beats.scene: Galaxies drawn as dots with arrows showing them moving away from each other
beats.summary: Question two: how did it begin? In the 1920s, scientists found that distant galaxies are moving away from us.

beats.scene: A film running backwards shows galaxies falling together into one hot point
beats.summary: If the expansion is run backwards, everything was once hotter and denser, about 13.8 billion years ago.

beats.scene: Two engineers beside a huge horn-shaped radio antenna in a field
beats.summary: In 1965 two radio engineers found a faint glow coming from all directions, the leftover light of the early universe.

beats.scene: Glowing gas cools and forms the first atoms in a dark space
beats.summary: In the first minutes, hydrogen and helium formed, and about 380,000 years later the first atoms formed and light could travel freely.

beats.scene: A bright point expands outward on a dark empty background
beats.summary: The Big Bang was not an explosion in space but the expansion of space itself, and what came before is not known.

beats.scene: A close view of a hand with a magnified skin, then cells, then atoms
beats.summary: Question three: what is it all made of? Everything we can see is made of atoms.

beats.scene: A star glows while atoms of carbon and oxygen drift out from it
beats.summary: Hydrogen and helium came from the Big Bang, but heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were made inside stars.

beats.scene: A galaxy spins with its outer stars moving as fast as the inner ones
beats.summary: In the 1970s, Vera Rubin found that stars at the edge of galaxies orbit too fast, which suggests extra unseen matter.

beats.scene: A glowing galaxy sits inside a huge dark invisible ball of mass
beats.summary: Dark matter, about a quarter of the universe, has never been seen directly and is known only by its gravity.

beats.scene: A pie chart shows five percent ordinary matter and the rest dark
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five percent of the universe, dark matter about twenty-seven and dark energy about sixty-eight.

beats.scene: A galaxy field with arrows showing the distances between galaxies growing faster
beats.summary: Question four: how will it end? In 1998 astronomers found that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

beats.scene: An old red star slowly fades beside a young blue one
beats.summary: Stars will eventually run out of gas, and the smallest red stars may shine for trillions of years.

beats.scene: A lone galaxy drifts in a dark, nearly empty sky
beats.summary: Because of dark energy, distant galaxies will move beyond sight, and in the far future the night sky may be almost empty.

beats.scene: Three different paths for the future of the universe drawn on a chart
beats.summary: The ending depends on dark energy, and scientists have several ideas, including a cold and dark universe or a faster tearing apart, but they do not know.

beats.scene: A calm sunrise over a field with a bright Sun in the sky
beats.summary: None of this will happen soon: the Sun will shine for about five billion more years.

beats.scene: A clock hangs in the dark among stars with a stretched face
beats.summary: Question five: what is time? We feel it pass at the same speed for everyone, but it does not.

beats.scene: Two clocks, one on a fast rocket ticking slower than one on the ground
beats.summary: A clock moving fast ticks more slowly than one that is still, and experiments with precise clocks confirm it.

beats.scene: A mountain-top clock and a sea-level clock beside a planet showing gravity
beats.summary: Gravity also slows time, so a clock on a mountain ticks very slightly faster than one at sea level.

beats.scene: A cup falls and breaks on a floor, shown again unbroken in reverse
beats.summary: Time seems to run in only one direction because disorder tends to increase: eggs break, but never mend themselves.

beats.scene: A traveller steps from a fast spaceship into a quiet garden years later
beats.summary: Travelling into the future is possible in a tiny way, but nobody knows a way to travel into the past.

beats.scene: An apple falls from a tree while the Moon hangs in the sky
beats.summary: Question six: what is gravity? Isaac Newton saw that the same pull makes things fall and keeps the Moon in orbit.

beats.scene: A heavy ball sinks into a stretched sheet while a small ball circles it
beats.summary: Einstein explained gravity as the bending of space and time by mass, as a heavy ball bends a stretched sheet.

beats.scene: Astronomers photograph stars near the dark disc of the Sun during an eclipse
beats.summary: In 1919, during a solar eclipse, astronomers saw that starlight bends as it passes the Sun, as Einstein predicted.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together sending ripples through a grid of space
beats.summary: In 2015, scientists detected gravitational waves, ripples in space made by two black holes crashing together.

beats.scene: A magnet lifts a small pin against the pull of a whole planet
beats.summary: Gravity is the weakest of the forces, yet it shapes the cosmos, and nobody has yet joined it with quantum physics.

beats.scene: A telescope points at a distant star with a small planet crossing it
beats.summary: Question seven: are there other Earths? The first planet around a Sun-like star was found in 1995.

beats.scene: A star dims slightly as a dark planet passes across its face
beats.summary: Astronomers find many planets by watching a star dim slightly as a planet passes in front of it.

beats.scene: A catalogue wall of many different planets, hot, icy, rocky and gassy
beats.summary: More than five thousand exoplanets are known, and they are much more varied than the planets of our Solar System.

beats.scene: A small blue-green planet floats in the narrow band where water can be liquid
beats.summary: Some rocky planets of about Earth's size orbit in the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist, but being in the zone does not mean being like Earth.

beats.scene: A giant telescope reads the colours of light from a distant planet's air
beats.summary: Telescopes can already study the air of some planets by analysing starlight, and they are getting better.

beats.scene: A planet with a green and blue surface sits alone beside a bright star
beats.summary: Question eight: are we alone? Nobody knows, because we have found life in only one place.

beats.scene: A rocky shore at dawn with early microscopic life in a shallow pool
beats.summary: Life began on Earth early, perhaps within a few hundred million years of the oceans, which hints that it may not be too hard, but is not proof.

beats.scene: A rover drives across red Martian ground beside a frozen moon with cracks
beats.summary: Within our Solar System, scientists look for signs of life, past or present, on Mars and on icy moons such as Europa and Enceladus.

beats.scene: A big radio dish points at the night sky while a computer shows signals
beats.summary: Since 1960, scientists have listened with radio telescopes for signals from other civilisations, and they have heard nothing clear.

beats.scene: A crowd of stars with one question mark floating among them
beats.summary: There are good reasons to think life elsewhere is possible, but the real answer is unknown, and the search goes on.

beats.scene: A giant star collapses into a dark circle with bright gas swirling around it
beats.summary: Question nine: what is a black hole? When a very massive star dies, its core can collapse into one.

beats.scene: A dark sphere with a thin circle marking the point of no return
beats.summary: A black hole's edge is called the event horizon, and nothing that crosses it can return.

beats.scene: A glowing orange ring surrounds a dark centre in a famous picture
beats.summary: In 2019 astronomers produced the first image of a black hole's shadow, in a galaxy called M87, and in 2022 one of our own galaxy's black hole.

beats.scene: An astronaut near a dark sphere with a clock slowing and her body stretched
beats.summary: Near a black hole, time slows, and a falling object would be stretched by the changing pull of gravity.

beats.scene: A dark centre with a question mark where the maths breaks down
beats.summary: What is inside a black hole is not known, because our theories of gravity and of the very small fail there.

beats.scene: A scientist writes a long question on a board covered with notes
beats.summary: Question ten: what don't we know? Science works by asking questions and testing the answers.

beats.scene: A telescope, a camera and a space probe lined up beneath the stars
beats.summary: Nearly everything we know about the universe comes from studying light and other signals with telescopes and probes.

beats.scene: A long list of questions glows on a night sky, including dark matter
beats.summary: Big unknowns include what dark matter and dark energy are, what happened before the Big Bang, how life began, and how gravity works at the smallest scale.

beats.scene: A door opens onto a larger room full of stars
beats.summary: Each answer has opened new questions: the story of science is a story of better questions.

beats.scene: A child stands under the night sky, looking up with a telescope
beats.summary: We are a small part of the universe able to wonder about it, and the questions are open to anyone.

B1B2: Some questions are so big that children ask them easily, and adults forget to. This book asks ten of them, and the first is the simplest: how big is the universe?
The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres from us, and the Sun is about 150 million kilometres away. Even these distances are already too big to imagine easily.
Light is the fastest thing there is, and in one year it travels about nine and a half trillion kilometres. Astronomers call this distance a light-year, and they use it as a ruler for the stars.
Our Sun belongs to a great spiral of stars called the Milky Way galaxy. It is about 100,000 light-years across, and it holds hundreds of billions of stars.

A telescope pointed at a tiny patch of dark sky once showed thousands of galaxies. The part of the universe we can see is about 93 billion light-years across, but the whole universe may be much larger.

The second question is how everything began, and the first clue came in the 1920s. Astronomers noticed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it goes.
If we run the expansion backwards like a film, the galaxies come closer and closer together. Almost fourteen billion years ago, everything was extremely hot and squeezed into a tiny space.

In 1965, two radio engineers were trying to remove a strange hiss from their antenna. The noise came from every direction in the sky, and it turned out to be the faint leftover light of the early universe.
In the first few minutes, the simplest atoms, hydrogen and helium, were formed. About 380,000 years later, the universe had cooled enough for atoms to form, and light could finally travel freely.
The Big Bang was not an explosion at one place in space. It was the start of the expansion of space itself, and nobody yet knows what came before it, or even whether that question makes sense.
Our third question is what everything is made of. The answer for the world we can see is atoms, so tiny that millions of them would fit across a hair.
The Big Bang made only hydrogen and helium, and a little else. Heavier atoms, such as the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body, were made inside stars and later thrown out into space.
In the 1970s, an astronomer named Vera Rubin measured how fast stars move in galaxies. Those at the edges move faster than the visible matter can explain, so something unseen must be pulling them.
Scientists call the unseen material dark matter, and it makes up about a quarter of the universe. We know it only by the pull of its gravity, because nobody has detected it directly.
The stars, planets and people are only about five percent of the universe. About 27 percent is dark matter, and the other 68 percent is something called dark energy, which we will meet next.
The fourth question is how the universe will end. In 1998, astronomers found something surprising: the expansion is not slowing down, but speeding up, as if something is pushing space apart.
New stars need clouds of gas, and the supply is slowly being used up. The smallest stars burn their fuel so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years.
If the expansion keeps speeding up, distant galaxies will slip out of view one by one. In the very far future, an observer might see only their own galaxy in a dark sky.
The ending depends on what dark energy is, and nobody can be sure yet. Many scientists expect a slow, cold fading, while a few ideas suggest something more dramatic.
None of this will happen for an enormously long time. The Sun is about halfway through its life and will shine for about five billion more years.
The fifth question is what time really is, and the answer is strange. It seems to move steadily for everybody, but about a hundred years ago a scientist named Einstein showed that it does not.
According to Einstein, a clock that moves very fast ticks more slowly than one standing still. Experiments with very exact clocks on aeroplanes and in orbit have confirmed it.
Gravity changes time as well, because the stronger the gravity, the more slowly a clock ticks. A clock on a mountain top therefore runs very slightly faster than one at sea level.

We remember the past and not the future, and physicists link this to disorder. A dropped cup breaks into pieces, but the pieces never jump back together, because there are more ways to be broken than whole.
In a very small way, astronauts do travel into the future, because their clocks tick a little slower. Travelling into the past, however, has never been seen, and no one knows how it could be done.
The sixth question is about gravity and why things fall. About 350 years ago, Isaac Newton realised that the force that makes an apple fall also keeps the Moon moving around the Earth.
In 1915, Einstein gave the world a new picture of gravity. Mass bends space and time, a little like a heavy ball on a stretched sheet, and smaller things roll along the curves.
Einstein's idea made a clear prediction: light should bend near the Sun. In 1919, during a solar eclipse, astronomers measured exactly that, and the news made him famous.
Einstein also predicted ripples in space, called gravitational waves. In 2015, scientists detected them for the first time, from two black holes that crashed together over a billion years ago.
Gravity is the weakest of nature's forces, as a small magnet can lift a pin against the pull of the whole Earth. Yet it shapes planets, stars and galaxies, and it still has secrets.
The seventh question is whether there are other worlds like ours. Planets around other stars are called exoplanets, and the first one orbiting a Sun-like star was found in 1995.
One way to find planets is to watch a star carefully. If a planet passes in front of it, the star gets a tiny bit dimmer, and the dip repeats every time the planet goes round.
More than 5,000 exoplanets are now known to us, and many are very different from ours. Some are giant planets that orbit closer to their star than Mercury is to the Sun.
A few planets are about the size of Earth and orbit where it is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water. However, that does not mean that they are like our home.
When starlight passes through a planet's air, the gases leave marks in the light. Telescopes can read these marks, and they have already found water vapour and other gases on several planets.
The eighth question is whether we are alone in the universe. The honest answer is that nobody knows, because we have found life in only one place, our own planet.
On Earth, life seems to have appeared fairly early, perhaps within a few hundred million years of the first oceans. That hints that life may not be impossibly hard to start, but it proves nothing.
Scientists look for signs of life in our own Solar System. Mars once had water on its surface, and the icy moons Europa and Enceladus have oceans of liquid water hidden under their ice.
Since 1960, scientists have used radio telescopes to listen for signals from other civilisations. So far, in more than sixty years, they have not found a clear message from anyone.
With so many stars and planets, many scientists think life elsewhere is likely, but a thought is not evidence. The real answer is unknown, and so the search goes on.
The ninth question is what a black hole is. When a very massive star runs out of fuel, its core can collapse, and the result is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing escapes.
The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon. Anything that goes past this line, even light, cannot come back out, because it would need to move faster than light.

In 2019, astronomers shared the first picture of a black hole, in a distant galaxy called M87. They joined together telescopes around the world, and in 2022 they produced one of the black hole in our own galaxy.
Close to a black hole, time runs more slowly, as relativity predicts. An object falling in would also be stretched, because the pull on its near side is much stronger than on its far side.

Nobody knows what lies inside a black hole, because no signal can come out. Our best theory predicts a point of endless density, but scientists think the theory breaks down there, and that a better one is needed.
The last question is what we still do not know. Science is not a list of answers, but a way of asking questions, testing ideas, and changing them when new evidence appears.
Almost everything we know about faraway places has come from light. Telescopes gather it, and tools called spectrographs split it into colours that show what the stars are made of.
Many big questions are still open, such as what dark matter and dark energy are. Nobody yet knows how life began or what happened before the Big Bang.

In science, every answer leads to new questions, and that is a sign of progress. A hundred years ago nobody knew that other galaxies existed, and today we are asking what most of the universe is made of.
You are a tiny part of the universe, and yet you can ask questions about it. Every one of these ten questions is waiting for the next person who is curious enough to look up.
C1C2: Some questions are so large that children ask them without any embarrassment, and adults slowly forget how. This book takes ten of them in turn, and for each one it tells you what scientists know, how they came to know it, and where their knowledge stops. The first question is the simplest of all, and it is also one of the hardest to answer: how big is the universe?

The Moon, our nearest neighbour, is about 384,000 kilometres away, and the Sun lies some 150 million kilometres out, nearly four hundred times farther. Even these distances, which are tiny by cosmic standards, are already too large for most people to picture. A jet aeroplane flying without a pause would need about nineteen years to reach the Sun.

Light is the fastest thing in the universe, and in a single year it covers about nine and a half trillion kilometres. Astronomers call this distance a light-year and use it as a ruler for the heavens, because ordinary units would give numbers so long that they would be useless. The nearest star beyond the Sun is a little over four light-years away, so the light that reaches us tonight left it more than four years ago.

Our Sun is one star among hundreds of billions that make up the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy roughly 100,000 light-years across. On a dark night, the pale band that crosses the sky is simply the combined light of the stars in our own galaxy, seen edge-on from the inside. Each of those faint points of light is a sun, and many of them have planets of their own.

When a space telescope stared for days at a tiny patch of apparently empty sky, no bigger than a grain of sand held at arm's length, it revealed thousands of galaxies. The part of the universe that we can possibly observe is about 93 billion light-years across and holds hundreds of billions of galaxies. Beyond that horizon, space may continue for a vast distance or even without end, but nobody can see it, so nobody can say.

The second question is how everything began, and the first clue arrived in the 1920s. Astronomers studying the light from other galaxies found that nearly all of them are moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy lies, the faster it seems to retreat. It was one of the most surprising discoveries in the history of science, and it overturned the old idea of a universe that never changes.

If we play the expansion backwards like a film, the galaxies draw closer and closer, the space between them shrinks, and the whole universe becomes hotter and denser. Almost fourteen billion years ago, it was so hot and so compressed that not even atoms could exist. This is the Big Bang theory, and it is supported by several independent kinds of evidence, which we shall meet next.

In 1965, two radio engineers tried everything to get rid of a persistent hiss in their giant antenna, even cleaning out the pigeon droppings. The noise came from every direction in the sky, and it proved to be the cool, faint afterglow of the early universe, now called the cosmic microwave background. The discovery, made almost by accident, was powerful evidence that the universe had begun hot and dense.

Within the first few minutes, the young universe cooled enough for the simplest kinds of atoms, hydrogen and helium, to be formed. After about 380,000 years it was cool enough for electrons to settle into atoms, and light was at last free to travel across space, and this is the light that we still detect today. Every galaxy, star and planet has grown from that early hydrogen and helium, drawn together slowly by gravity over countless ages.

The name is misleading, for the Big Bang was not an explosion at one point in a space that already existed. It marks the moment when space itself began to expand, everywhere at once, and what lay before it, if the question even makes sense, remains one of the great unknowns of science. Honest researchers have theories about it, but they have no proof, and they say so plainly.

The third question is what everything is made of, and for the world that we can see and touch, the answer is atoms. They are so small that millions of them would fit across the width of a single hair, and each is built from a tiny nucleus surrounded by a cloud of electrons. Inside, an atom is almost entirely empty space, so you are far less solid than you feel.

The Big Bang made almost nothing but hydrogen and helium, so every heavier element had to be made later. The carbon in your cells, the oxygen in your lungs and the iron in your blood were all forged inside stars, and scattered into space when those stars grew old and died. Except for hydrogen, you are therefore made of material that was once part of an ancient star.

In the 1970s, the American astronomer Vera Rubin measured the speeds of stars as they orbit the centres of their galaxies, and found a puzzle. The stars at the outer edges move much faster than the visible matter could possibly hold in place, as though some unseen material were adding its pull. Other observations soon pointed the same way, and the idea of dark matter was taken seriously.

The unseen material is called dark matter, and it seems to make up about a quarter of everything in the universe, more than five times as much as ordinary matter. We know of it only through its gravity, since it neither shines nor blocks light, and experiments designed to catch its particles have not yet succeeded. It is one of the biggest open problems in modern physics, and a great many researchers are working on it.

Everything that you have ever seen, including every planet, star and person, adds up to only about five percent of the universe. Roughly 27 percent is dark matter, and about 68 percent is a mysterious something called dark energy, though these percentages are estimates and may change. In other words, science can describe the visible part very well while still knowing very little about the rest.

The fourth question is how it will all end, and the answer depends on a discovery made in 1998. Astronomers measuring distant exploding stars expected to find that the expansion of the universe was slowing down under the pull of gravity, but they found the opposite. It is speeding up, and the cause was named dark energy even though nobody knows what it is.

New stars can only form from clouds of gas, and the supply of that gas is steadily being used up. The smallest stars burn their fuel so slowly that they may shine for trillions of years, but eventually even the last of them will fade, and the universe will become much darker. The age of stars, scientists say, is only a small part of the story.

If the acceleration continues, distant galaxies will move away so fast that their light will never reach us, and they will slip out of view one by one. In the very far future, a lonely astronomer might see nothing at all beyond the stars of her own galaxy, and she might never guess that the universe was once crowded with others. We are, in this sense, lucky to be alive in an age when the evidence is still visible.

The final fate depends on what dark energy really is, and on that point the evidence is still incomplete. The most widely held expectation is a long, cold fading in which everything spreads out and cools towards darkness, though other ideas suggest a violent tearing apart or a sudden change. Future measurements may help to choose among them, but for now science honestly cannot say.

None of this is anything to worry about, since these changes unfold over spans of time that dwarf human history. The Sun is about halfway through its life and has roughly five billion years of shining still to come, and even that is a mere moment compared with the end of the universe. Our own species, by comparison, has existed for only a few hundred thousand years.

The fifth question is what time really is, and it is a more slippery question than it seems. To us it seems to move at the same steady pace for everyone, like a river that carries all of us along together, but about a hundred years ago Albert Einstein showed that this is not quite true. His theory of relativity changed the way scientists think about space and time, and its strange predictions have been tested many times since.

According to relativity, a clock that is moving fast ticks more slowly than one that stays still, and extremely precise clocks flown on aeroplanes and in orbit have confirmed it. The effect is far too small for us to notice at ordinary speeds, since it only becomes dramatic as the speed approaches that of light. It is not a trick of the instruments: time itself really does pass differently.

Gravity affects time too, so that a clock ticks slightly more slowly where gravity is stronger, and a clock on a mountain top runs a tiny bit faster than the same clock at sea level. The difference is incredibly small, but modern atomic clocks can detect it, even over a height of only a few centimetres. The navigation satellites that guide our phones must correct for both effects, or they would soon go badly wrong.

We remember the past but never the future, and physicists link this strange one-way flow to disorder. A dropped cup shatters into hundreds of pieces, yet the pieces never leap back together, because there are overwhelmingly more ways of being broken than of being whole. The laws of physics do not clearly explain why time has a direction, and so the arrow of time is still an open puzzle.

In a very small way, travel to the future is real: astronauts on the space station age a fraction of a second less than people on the ground, because they are moving fast. Travel into the past is quite another matter, since there is no evidence that it is possible, and it would raise deep problems about cause and effect. For now, the future is the only direction in which we can move at all.

The sixth question is about gravity, the force that makes a dropped apple fall to the ground. In the late seventeenth century Isaac Newton realised that the very same pull holds the Moon in its path around the Earth, and keeps the planets circling the Sun. It was the first time anyone had shown that the same law rules both the earth and the sky.

In 1915, Einstein offered a very different picture of gravity, in which mass bends space and time around it. A heavy ball resting on a stretched rubber sheet is a fair image: a smaller ball passing nearby will roll along the curve, not because it is pulled by some mysterious force, but because the sheet itself is bent. Planets orbit the Sun because they follow the curves that the Sun makes in space and time.

Einstein's theory made a bold, testable prediction, that the Sun should bend the light of stars passing close to it. In 1919, during a total eclipse of the Sun, astronomers photographed stars near its edge and found them shifted by the amount he had predicted. The announcement made the front pages of newspapers, and it showed how a theory can be proved by a daring measurement.

Relativity also predicted that moving masses should send ripples through space, and in 2015 scientists detected one for the first time. The waves came from two black holes that had spiralled together and merged more than a billion years earlier, and they stretched and squeezed the detectors by less than the width of an atom's nucleus. It was like hearing the universe speak in a new language, and astronomers have since heard many more such signals.

Gravity is by far the weakest of the forces of nature, as a small magnet shows when it lifts a pin against the pull of the whole Earth. Even so, it gathers gas into stars and stars into galaxies, and over great distances it always wins. Physicists have not yet managed to combine it with quantum theory, the successful description of the very small, and it remains an unsolved problem.

The seventh question is whether other worlds like ours exist, and it was long a matter of pure opinion. For most of history nobody could see a planet around another star, but in 1995 astronomers found the first one circling a star like the Sun. Planets outside our Solar System are now called exoplanets, and the search for them has become one of the busiest and most exciting fields in astronomy.

One of the most successful methods is to watch a star very carefully for a slight dimming. If a planet passes in front of it, a little of the light is blocked, and because the dip repeats each time the planet orbits, astronomers can work out its size and the length of its year. Telescopes in space have used this patient trick to find thousands of worlds, most of which nobody had imagined.

More than five thousand exoplanets have now been confirmed, and they are far more varied than anything in our own Solar System. There are giant planets that circle their stars in just a few days, worlds that may be covered by deep oceans, and rocky planets that orbit so close that their surfaces are hot enough to melt metal. Astronomers now think that most stars have planets of some kind, which is a very different picture from the one that scientists held a generation ago.

A few rocky planets of about Earth's size orbit within the habitable zone, the range of distances where liquid water could exist on a surface. This is only a first clue, however, since a planet's air, its weather and its history decide whether it is truly comfortable. Venus and Mars both lie near the edges of our own Sun's habitable zone, and neither is welcoming.

When starlight filters through the air of a planet, the gases in it leave faint dark marks in the spectrum, rather like fingerprints. The newest space telescopes can read some of these marks, and they have already detected water vapour, carbon dioxide and other gases around several planets. Within a few decades they may be able to study the air of planets that are much like ours.

The eighth question is the one that people most want answered: are we alone? The honest reply is that nobody knows, because life has so far been found in a single place, our own planet, and one example is not enough to say how common it is. Whatever the truth turns out to be, it will profoundly change how we see ourselves, and our place in the cosmos.

On Earth, life seems to have started fairly soon after the planet had cooled enough to hold oceans, perhaps within a few hundred million years. A quick start hints that the step might not be impossibly difficult, but it proves nothing, because we are the survivors of one single experiment. We cannot rule out that Earth was extraordinarily lucky, and equally we cannot rule out that it was ordinary.

Closer to home, scientists search for signs of life, past or present, on Mars, where rivers and lakes once flowed, and on icy moons such as Europa and Enceladus, which hide oceans of liquid water beneath their crusts. So far nobody has found anything convincing, and finding even a single microbe would be among the greatest discoveries in history. It would suggest that life begins easily whenever the conditions are right, and that the galaxy may be full of it.

Since 1960, scientists have pointed radio telescopes at nearby stars and listened for signals that could only have been made by technology. In more than sixty years of searching they have found nothing that has survived careful checking, though they have covered only a small portion of the possible frequencies and stars. The silence tells us something, but it is far from the final word, and the search is becoming more powerful every year.

With hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy alone, many scientists suspect that life exists elsewhere, at least in simple forms, but a hunch is not evidence. Others point out that intelligent life may be rare, or that distances may simply make contact impossible. Both views are reasonable, and only observations will settle the argument, so the search continues.

The ninth question concerns the strangest objects known to science, which are the black holes. When a very massive star runs out of fuel, its core can collapse under its own weight into a region so dense that its gravity allows nothing to escape, not even light. The star's outer layers are blown away in a great explosion, and what remains at the centre is a black hole.

The boundary of a black hole is known as the event horizon, and it is the point of no return. Anything that crosses it, including light, is trapped, since escaping would require a speed greater than the speed of light, and nothing can reach that. The black hole itself is not a hole in the usual sense but a place with so much mass in so little space that everything near it falls inward.

In 2019, a team of astronomers released the first image of a black hole, a glowing ring of hot gas around a dark shadow at the heart of a galaxy called M87. They had linked radio telescopes across the world to make a single instrument the size of the Earth, and in 2022 they did the same for the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy. A thing that cannot be seen had at last been photographed by the glow of its surroundings, which is a remarkable achievement.

Close to a black hole, time runs more and more slowly, and a distant observer would see a falling clock tick slower and slower until it seemed to freeze at the horizon. The traveller herself would notice nothing odd about her own clock, but the pull on her feet would be stronger than on her head, and she would be gently, then violently, stretched. This is not a fate that anyone is likely to test, since the nearest known black hole is thousands of light-years away.

Nobody knows what lies inside a black hole, since no signal from within can reach us. Relativity predicts that everything falls towards a point of infinite density, called a singularity, but most physicists take this as a sign that the theory breaks down, and that a better description of gravity is needed. A black hole is therefore a place where our understanding runs out, and where the next great discovery may be waiting.

The tenth and last question asks what we still do not know, and it may be the most important. Science is not a fixed list of answers but a way of asking questions, testing the replies against evidence, and changing course when the evidence demands it. An honest scientist is never embarrassed to say that she does not know yet.

Almost everything we know about faraway places has come to us as light, which telescopes gather and instruments split into its colours. From those colours astronomers can read the chemical makeup, the temperature, the speed and even the age of a distant star. We have never visited a single star besides our Sun, yet we know a great deal about thousands of them.

Many of the biggest questions remain open: what dark matter and dark energy truly are, how life began, what happened before the Big Bang, and how gravity behaves at the smallest scales. Each of them has been argued over by talented people for decades, and none has yet been settled. It is wise to hold firmly onto what is well tested, and loosely onto what is merely suggested.

In science, each answer tends to open a door onto a bigger room, and that is how progress happens. A hundred years ago many astronomers thought that the Milky Way was the whole universe, and today we are asking what most of the cosmos is made of. This is not a failure of science but its greatest strength, because each new question that we can ask is a sign of something that we have learned.

You are a very small part of the universe, assembled from atoms forged in ancient stars, and yet you are able to look up and ask about the whole. Every one of these ten questions is still waiting for someone curious and patient enough to push the answer a little further. Perhaps that person will be you, and if not, there is still no more fitting way to spend a clear night than in quiet wonder.
